title: Explicit matrix models for reductive groups of semisimple rank one
statement: Let $F$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Use reductivity, maximal tori, and scheme-theoretic centralizer points as in [def-sfb-reductive-torus-centralizer-terminology]. A torus is a group isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m^r$ for an integer $r\geq0$, where $\mathbf G_m(A)=A^\times$ [def-sc-gm-ga]. Let $H$ be reductive, let $T\subseteq H$ be a maximal torus, and let $R\subseteq H$ be the largest smooth connected solvable normal subgroup, and assume that the fppf quotient $H/R$ has maximal tori of dimension one. Here solvable means that successive commutator subgroup schemes eventually become trivial, and the quotient is the represented fppf quotient of [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry]. Then the pair $(H,T)$ is isomorphic over $F$ to one of the pairs $$\bigl(\mathbf G_m^r\times\operatorname{SL}_2,\mathbf G_m^r\times D_{\mathrm{SL}}\bigr),\quad \bigl(\mathbf G_m^r\times\operatorname{PGL}_2,\mathbf G_m^r\times D_{\mathrm{PGL}}\bigr),\quad \bigl(\mathbf G_m^r\times\operatorname{GL}_2,\mathbf G_m^r\times D_{\mathrm{GL}}\bigr)$$ for some integer $r\geq0$. Here $\operatorname{GL}_2(A)$ is the invertible $2\times2$ matrices, $\operatorname{SL}_2(A)$ the determinant-one matrices, and $\operatorname{PGL}_2$ the fppf sheaf quotient of $\operatorname{GL}_2$ by scalar matrices; fppf sheafification is for faithfully flat finitely presented coverings of commutative $F$-algebras. The subgroups $D_{\mathrm{SL}}$, $D_{\mathrm{PGL}}$, and $D_{\mathrm{GL}}$ are respectively the diagonal determinant-one matrices, the images of diagonal invertible matrices, and all diagonal invertible matrices. Under these isomorphisms the derived subgroup $H^{\mathrm{der}}$ is respectively $1\times\operatorname{SL}_2$, $1\times\operatorname{PGL}_2$, and $1\times\operatorname{SL}_2\subseteq\mathbf G_m^r\times\operatorname{GL}_2$. The derived subgroup means the smallest closed subgroup through which the commutator morphism factors. The classification holds in every characteristic, including characteristic two.

source.place: Theorem 20.33 and Corollary 20.34, printed pp.418--419; Proposition 20.24 (perfectness of SL2 and PGL2), printed p.416; Proposition 20.32 (derived group), printed pp.418--419. Theorem 20.33 is read with its semisimple-rank-one hypothesis, as the errata specify; the derived-group cases are corrected to agree with the displayed products.

proof.text: Put $S=\operatorname{SL}_{2,F}$. By [lem-sfb-sl2-universal-multiplicative-cover] it is semisimple and its scalar quotient is the universal multiplicative covering of $\operatorname{PGL}_2$. We first verify that $S$ is perfect, without using any general root-datum theorem. An algebraically closed field is infinite (a finite field would make $\prod_{c\in F}(X-c)-1$ a polynomial with no root); choose $a\ne0$ with $a^2\ne1$. Apply [lem-sfb-sl2-field-commutator-generation]. By [lem-sfb-smooth-connected-derived-subgroup], $S^{\mathrm{der}}(F)=[S(F),S(F)]=S(F)$. The coordinate ring $F[x,y,z,w]/(xw-yz-1)$ is reduced: the opens where $x$ or $z$ is invertible cover it, since $xw-yz=1$, and each is a Laurent polynomial ring over $F$. Every function in the ideal of $S^{\mathrm{der}}$ therefore vanishes on all $F$-points and is zero by [lem-wf-affine-nullstellensatz-vanishing]. Thus $S^{\mathrm{der}}=S$ as schemes.

source.place: Propositions 20.24 and 20.31, pp.416,418; the point-to-scheme argument of 20.24 is supplied explicitly.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-rank-one-adjoint-projective-linear] to $H$: the assumed rank of $H/R$ is exactly its hypothesis, so $H/Z(H)\simeq\operatorname{PGL}_2$. Transport the covering from step 1 along this isomorphism. Apply [lem-sfb-reductive-central-pushout-reconstruction] with this perfect semisimple $S$. We obtain a diagonalizable $D=Z(H)$, a homomorphism $\varphi:\mu_2\to D$ with torus cokernel, and $$H\simeq(S\times D)/\{(\epsilon I_2,\varphi(\epsilon)^{-1}):\epsilon^2=1\}.$$ The image of $S$ in this quotient is precisely $H^{\mathrm{der}}$. All kernels and quotients here are schematic/fppf; in characteristic two none is replaced by its set of field points.

source.place: Remark 19.30, pp.404--405, and the opening of the proof of Theorem 20.33, p.419; use the noninjective version of the centre map.

proof.text: Use [lem-sfb-multiplicative-character-antiduality]. Write $D=D_F(M)$ and $\alpha=\varphi^*:M\to\mathbf Z/2\mathbf Z$, since $\mu_2=D_F(\mathbf Z/2\mathbf Z)$. Contravariant equivalence takes the cokernel of $\varphi$ to the kernel $K=\ker\alpha$; explicitly a character factors through $D/\operatorname{im}\varphi$ exactly when its restriction to $\mu_2$ is zero. That cokernel is a torus, so $K$ is free of finite rank. Its finite basis can equivalently be chosen using [lem-trf-fg-torsionfree-group-free]. There are two possibilities for $\alpha$: zero, or surjective. No surjectivity is presumed in advance.

source.place: Theorem 12.9 and the character calculation in the proof of Theorem 20.33, p.419, corrected to allow alpha = 0.

proof.text: If $\alpha=0$, then $M=K$ and $D\simeq\mathbf G_m^r$; antiduality says $\varphi$ is the trivial homomorphism. The quotient of step 2 is consequently $\mathbf G_m^r\times(S/\mu_2)=\mathbf G_m^r\times\operatorname{PGL}_2$, using [lem-sfb-projective-matrix-central-cover] with matrix size two. The image of $S$ is exactly the second factor, so the derived subgroup has the required description.

source.place: The second character case of Theorem 20.33, p.419, and the scalar quotient of Example 5.49.

proof.text: Now suppose $\alpha$ is onto and choose $m\in M$ with $\alpha(m)=1$. Then $M$ is generated by $K$ and $m$, with its sole extra relation $2m=k_0$ for $k_0\in K$: every relation has an even coefficient of $m$ and reduces to this one. Choose a basis of the finite free group $K$. If $k_0\in2K$, replace $m$ by $m-k_0/2$; then $M=K\oplus\langle m\rangle$ with $2m=0$ and $\alpha$ the projection to $\mathbf Z/2$. Otherwise the coordinate vector of $k_0$ is nonzero modulo two. Swap a nonzero coordinate to the first position, and subtract that coordinate from every other odd coordinate by integral basis operations. The vector is now $(1,0,\ldots,0)$ modulo two. Replacing $m$ by $m+k$ changes $k_0$ by $2k$, so arrange $2m=e_1$. Eliminating $e_1$ gives $M=\mathbf Zm\oplus\bigoplus_{i>1}\mathbf Ze_i$, with $\alpha(m)=1$ and $\alpha(e_i)=0$. This exhaustive calculation also handles $K=0$, where only the first case occurs.

source.place: The two nonzero character cases of Theorem 20.33, p.419; the finite-lattice calculation is written out.

proof.text: In the case $M=K\oplus\mathbf Z/2$, character antiduality identifies $D$ with $\mathbf G_m^r\times\mu_2$ and $\varphi$ with the inclusion into the last factor. The map $$(s,t,z)\longmapsto(t,zs)$$ identifies the quotient in step 2 with $\mathbf G_m^r\times S$: it has inverse $(t,s)\mapsto[(s,t,1)]$, and its kernel is exactly $(\epsilon I_2,1,\epsilon^{-1})$. These formulas work on all algebra-valued points, including nilpotents. The image of $S$ is $1\times S$.

source.place: The first character case of Theorem 20.33, p.419; the quotient isomorphism is explicit.

proof.text: In the remaining case $M=N\oplus\mathbf Zm$ with $\alpha$ reduction on $m$, antiduality identifies $D$ with $D_F(N)\times\mathbf G_m=\mathbf G_m^r\times\mathbf G_m$ and $\varphi(\epsilon)=(1,\epsilon)$. The map $$(s,t,z)\longmapsto(t,zs)\in\mathbf G_m^r\times\operatorname{GL}_2$$ has kernel exactly $(\epsilon I_2,1,\epsilon^{-1})$. It is fppf locally surjective: for an invertible matrix $g$ over an algebra $B$, adjoining an invertible root $z$ of $z^2=\det g$ is a finite free faithfully flat cover of rank two; then $s=z^{-1}g$ has determinant one. Thus the represented quotient [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] identifies this quotient with $\mathbf G_m^r\times\operatorname{GL}_2$. The image of $S$ is exactly the determinant-one subgroup in the second factor. This calculation uses no division by two.

source.place: The third character case of Theorem 20.33, p.419; Example 19.28, p.405; scalar multiplication as in Example 19.24, p.404.

proof.text:
Let $f:H\simeq G$ be the resulting matrix-model isomorphism and let $D_G\subseteq G$ be the displayed diagonal subgroup ($\mathbf G_m^r$ times $D_{\mathrm{SL}}$, $D_{\mathrm{PGL}}$ or $D_{\mathrm{GL}}$). The image $f(T)$ is a maximal torus, since an isomorphism preserves inclusions of torus subgroups. The subgroup $D_G$ is a torus, isomorphic to $\mathbf G_m^{r+1}$, $\mathbf G_m^{r+1}$ (by $[\operatorname{diag}(a,b)]\mapsto a/b$, using [lem-sfb-projective-matrix-central-cover]) and $\mathbf G_m^{r+2}$. It is maximal. Let $j:S	o G$ be a closed torus inclusion and $D_G	o S$ a homomorphism compatible with the inclusions. Since $S$ is commutative, every $x\in S(F)$ commutes with $D_G(F)$. Write the matrix component of $x$ as $X=(x_{ij})$, a matrix over $F$; for $\operatorname{PGL}_2$ this is a lift, which exists and is unique up to $F^	imes$ because $\operatorname{GL}_2	o\operatorname{PGL}_2$ is a $\mathbf G_m$-torsor [lem-sfb-projective-matrix-central-cover] whose fibre over an $F$-point is a nonempty finite type $F$-scheme, hence has an $F$-point [lem-wf-affine-nullstellensatz-vanishing]. Choose $a\in F$ with $a
eq0$, $a^2
eq1$ as in step 1. Commuting with $\operatorname{diag}(a,a^{-1})$ (for $\operatorname{SL}_2$) or with $\operatorname{diag}(a,1)$ (for $\operatorname{GL}_2$) gives $a^{\pm2}x_{12}=x_{12}$, resp. $a^{\pm1}x_{12}=x_{12}$, and the same for $x_{21}$, so $X$ is diagonal. For $\operatorname{PGL}_2$, $\operatorname{diag}(a,1)X\operatorname{diag}(a,1)^{-1}=\lambda X$ with $\lambda\in F^	imes$, i.e. $x_{11}=\lambda x_{11}$, $x_{22}=\lambda x_{22}$, $ax_{12}=\lambda x_{12}$, $a^{-1}x_{21}=\lambda x_{21}$. If $x_{11}$ or $x_{22}$ is nonzero then $\lambda=1$ and $x_{12}=x_{21}=0$; otherwise $x_{12},x_{21}
e0$ by invertibility and $\lambda=a=a^{-1}$, contradicting $a^2
eq1$. Hence $S(F)\subseteq D_G(F)$. The coordinate ring of $S\simeq\mathbf G_m^s$ is a Laurent polynomial ring, hence reduced, so by [lem-wf-affine-nullstellensatz-vanishing](3) the closed immersion $j$ factors through the closed subgroup $D_G$. Thus $D_G\subseteq S\subseteq D_G$ as closed subschemes of $G$, and $D_G	o S$ is an isomorphism. Apply [lem-sfb-borel-maximal-torus-conjugacy] in the smooth connected group $G$ to obtain $g\in G(F)$ with $gf(T)g^{-1}=D_G$ as subgroup schemes. The isomorphism $\operatorname{inn}(g)\circ f$ is now an isomorphism of the required pairs. The derived subgroup descriptions from steps 4,6,7 persist under this conjugation, because a commutator subgroup is invariant under every inner automorphism.
